story.title: Appeals Court Provides Trump Opportunity to Challenge Hush Money Conviction
story.summary: A federal appeals court has ruled that Donald Trump can seek to move his hush money conviction case to federal court. The court found that a lower judge made an error in determining that Trump had delayed too long in raising his presidential immunity defense. If the case is moved, Trump could argue for the dismissal of the charges based on this immunity.

explore_lenses.label: How did the removal fight reach this point?
explore_lenses.title: A second removal bid followed the immunity ruling
explore_lenses.summary: Trump first tried to transfer the Manhattan case before trial; after the Supreme Court’s 2024 immunity decision, he sought permission for a second, late removal notice. The procedural dispute has centered on whether that delay was justified and whether removal remains available after conviction.

claims.text: Federal law generally requires a criminal defendant to file a removal notice within 30 days of arraignment or before trial, but permits a late filing for good cause; it also limits second notices to grounds that did not exist when the first was filed, subject to relief for good cause.
In August 2026, Hellerstein denied Trump leave to file a second notice, finding that the asserted grounds were neither new nor legally sufficient and that Trump had not shown good cause or diligence.

Manhattan prosecutors have argued that the charges concern falsified business records and private conduct, and that any federal-law challenge should proceed through New York’s appellate courts rather than by post-conviction removal.

explore_lenses.label: What happens to Trump’s state appeal now?
explore_lenses.title: The state appeal is paused while removal is addressed
explore_lenses.summary: Trump had separately pursued an ordinary appeal in New York state court. The Second Circuit asked that state-court proceedings stop while the federal removal question is pending, putting that track on hold for now.

claims.text: The Second Circuit instructed the district court to request that no further state-court proceedings occur while the removal issue is pending, a step intended to preserve the status quo.
Trump’s conventional state appeal had been argued before New York’s Appellate Division on November 5, 2026, but no ruling had issued before the federal appeals court’s November 23 order.

If removal is eventually permitted, the Second Circuit said the federal court should adopt the state-court judgment, after which Trump could press his federal immunity arguments against that judgment.

story_report.summary: A federal appeals court has reopened Donald Trump’s effort to shift his hush money conviction case from New York state court to federal court, ruling that a lower court wrongly treated post-conviction removal as categorically unavailable and improperly denied him leave to make a second attempt. The Second Circuit did not decide whether removal or presidential immunity ultimately applies. It instructed the district court to seek a pause in further state-court proceedings while the removal question is considered.

sections.heading: Trump Immunity Argument and Prosecutors’ Position
sections.body: Trump’s lawyers contend that trial evidence concerning his conduct as president was shielded by presidential immunity and that a federal court should resolve the issue. Manhattan prosecutors have maintained that the case concerns falsified business records and private conduct, arguing that any federal-law challenge should instead move through New York’s appellate courts. Judge Alvin Hellerstein had similarly concluded that the payments and alleged cover-up were private, unofficial conduct outside immunity protection.

sections.heading: Removal Deadlines and Prior Denial
sections.body: Federal law generally requires a criminal defendant seeking removal to file notice within 30 days of arraignment or before trial, though late filings may be permitted for good cause. It also restricts second removal notices to grounds unavailable when the first notice was filed, subject to good-cause relief. In August 2026, Hellerstein denied Trump permission to submit a second notice, finding his grounds neither new nor legally sufficient and concluding that he had not shown good cause or diligence.

sections.heading: Federal Review and State Appeal
sections.body: Trump’s conventional appeal was argued before New York’s Appellate Division on November 5, 2026, but no decision had been issued before the Second Circuit’s November 23 order. If removal is ultimately allowed, the appeals court said the federal court should adopt the state-court judgment, allowing Trump to press federal immunity arguments against it.

unresolved.text: The appeals court did not determine whether Trump’s conviction qualifies for removal or whether presidential immunity applies to it.
Further proceedings will determine the scope of the district court’s reconsideration, the judge assigned to the matter, and when the New York appeal may resume if removal is denied.

related_stories.title: India Commits $1.6 Billion in Flood Relief to Nepal During Prime Minister's Visit
related_stories.summary: India has pledged $1.6 billion in flood relief to Nepal as Prime Minister Balendra Shah visits New Delhi. This marks Shah's first international trip since taking office in March. The visit also resulted in agreements on infrastructure projects, including a railway and a hydropower plant.

related_stories.title: Trump Claims Role in Jensen Huang's Return to Nvidia Amid National Security Concerns
related_stories.summary: President Trump has claimed credit for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia, stating he communicated with the company's board to address concerns regarding national security. He emphasized that the government does not view Huang's return as a risk to national security and described the announcement as vital for Nvidia's success and the economy.
